title: From Grocery Lists to Gallery Walls: Marisa Aragón Ware’s Paper Sculptures Redefine the Everyday
summary:
Imagine holding a sheet of paper—the same kind you might scribble a homework reminder on—and turning it into a lifelike bird’s wing or a fragile wildflower. That’s the everyday magic Marisa Aragón Ware conjures in her Boulder studio. Growing up roaming the Rocky Mountain forests with her scientist father, Ware absorbed nature’s intricate patterns: the veins of a leaf, the curve of a bone, the layered barbs of a feather. Now, she channels that fascination into meticulously cut and scored paper sculptures that seem to breathe.

Ware’s choice of medium is deliberate. “Paper is deeply familiar—everyone has handled it, written grocery lists on it, folded it, torn it, discarded it,” she says. “Because it’s such an everyday material, there’s something especially powerful about transforming it into something unexpected.” Her process is painstaking: she carves delicate curves to mimic organic volume, etches precise lines to define insect wings or petals, and builds forms that echo the complexity of real specimens.

Underpinning her work is the theory of biophilia—the idea that humans have an innate urge to connect with nature. “Our need for nature extends far beyond physical survival; it also nourishes imagination, spirituality, and our sense of meaning,” Ware explains. Through her sculptures, she hopes to spark wonder and a desire to protect the natural world. Recently, she’s been loosening her approach, incorporating experimental techniques like cyanotypes and embracing a beginner’s mindset. “I’ve been asking myself what may have been lost in the process of becoming technically skilled,” she says.

You can catch Ware’s work in the group show “Common Waters” at Arch Enemy Arts, opening June 5. Follow her on Instagram for more of these stunning transformations.
why_it_matters: For a generation growing up with screens, Ware's work shows the power of hands-on making and the beauty of the natural world, urging us to see potential in the ordinary and to protect the environment that inspires such art.

background_read: Marisa Aragón Ware is a contemporary artist based in Boulder, Colorado, who transforms ordinary paper into intricate, lifelike sculptures. Her artistic philosophy is rooted in biophilia, a term coined by American biologist E.O. Wilson in 1984 to describe humans' instinctive connection to the natural world.

Paper art has a rich global history, from the ancient Chinese craft of jianzhi (paper cutting) to the modern, large-scale installations of Danish artist Peter Callesen, who also uses a single sheet of paper. Ware's recent experimentation with cyanotypes taps into one of the oldest photographic processes: invented by Sir John Herschel in 1842, cyanotypes produce a characteristic blue hue and were famously used by botanist Anna Atkins to document algae.

Her work is being shown at Arch Enemy Arts, a Philadelphia gallery celebrated for its pop-surrealism and illustration art, connecting her to a wider community of artists who blur the line between craft and high art.

perspectives.description: Ware’s work celebrates the humble material of paper, showing how it can be elevated into intricate art. Her biophilia-inspired sculptures remind viewers of the beauty and fragility of nature, potentially fostering a deeper appreciation for the environment.

Some might argue that paper sculptures are too delicate and impermanent, making them difficult to preserve or display widely. Additionally, the focus on hyper-detailed craft could overshadow conceptual depth, possibly limiting the work's broader meaning.

The use of biophilia in art reflects a larger cultural response to urbanization and nature deficit, where people seek connections to the natural world indoors. Ware’s transition to cyanotypes and a beginner's mindset mirrors a broader trend in contemporary art of embracing chance and imperfection after achieving technical mastery.

As Ware continues to experiment with photographic techniques, her work might bridge sculpture and two-dimensional imagery, opening new avenues for storytelling. If her approach inspires other artists or young students, it could spark a revival of paper arts and a stronger environmental message in visual culture.
